moments.title: Arithmetic or geometric?
moments.text: An arithmetic sequence changes by a constant difference; a geometric sequence uses a constant ratio.

moments.title: Identify the common difference
moments.text: In $-6,1,8,15,22,\ldots$, each term is 7 more than the preceding term, so $d=7$.

moments.title: Label the terms
moments.text: The presenter labels the first, second and third terms $u_1$, $u_2$ and $u_3$.

moments.title: A negative difference
moments.text: In $10,8,6,4,\ldots$, the common difference is $d=-2$.

moments.title: Formula booklet
moments.text: The presenter points out the arithmetic-sequence and series formulas before using them.

moments.title: Finding a distant term
moments.text: Listing many terms is inefficient, so use the term formula to find $u_{15}$.

moments.title: From a sequence to a series
moments.text: The presenter switches from finding an individual term to finding the sum of a number of terms.

moments.title: Set up the first ten terms
moments.text: The task is to add the first 10 terms, from $u_1$ through $u_{10}$.

moments.title: Use the sum formula
moments.text: Substitute $n=10$, $u_1=-6$ and $d=7$ into $S_n=\frac n2[2u_1+(n-1)d]$.

moments.title: The sum is 255
moments.text: The sum of the first ten terms is $S_{10}=255$.

moments.title: An alternative form
moments.text: When the first and last terms are known, use $S_n=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$; the presenter returns to this form near the end.

moments.title: Why use sigma notation?
moments.text: Sigma notation is a compact way to write the sum of a sequence of terms.

moments.title: Read the components
moments.text: The sigma indicates addition; the lower and upper limits specify where the index begins and ends.

moments.title: Set up the summand
moments.text: The first example is $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(k+3)$.

moments.title: Substitute each index
moments.text: Use $k=1,2,3,4$ in the expression $k+3$ and add the results.

moments.title: Evaluate the sum
moments.text: The terms are $4,5,6,7$, giving a total of 22.

moments.title: A different starting index
moments.text: The next example starts at $k=3$, not $k=1$, and ends at $k=6$.

moments.title: Write the four terms
moments.text: Substitute $k=3,4,5,6$ into $1/3^k$. Both limits are included.

notes.title: Check the lower limit
notes.text: The first example is written from $k=1$ to $k=4$. The spoken recap is easy to confuse with a different starting value.
notes.write: Use the limits shown in the expression: $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(k+3)=4+5+6+7=22$.

ican.text: I can identify an arithmetic sequence and find its first term and common difference.
I can use a term formula to find a term or solve for an unknown term number.
I can find a sum of consecutive arithmetic terms using an appropriate series formula.
I can read and evaluate sigma notation, including a starting index other than 1.
I can use an arithmetic model in context and interpret its assumptions.
I can use an approximate common difference to model imperfectly arithmetic data and make a qualified prediction.

ku.text: An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference $d=u_{n+1}-u_n$. The difference may be positive, negative or zero.
Starting with $u_1$, the $n$th term is $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$. There are $n-1$ changes between the first and $n$th terms.
The first $n$ terms sum to $S_n=\frac n2[2u_1+(n-1)d]=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$. The second form uses the first and last terms of the sum.
$u_n$ is one term; $S_n$ is the total of terms $u_1$ through $u_n$. To sum from $u_a$ to $u_b$, use $S_b-S_{a-1}$ or the number of terms $b-a+1$.
In $\sum_{k=a}^{b}f(k)$, substitute each integer from $a$ through $b$ into $f(k)$ and add. The limits are inclusive.
When a context asks for the first term exceeding a target, solve the inequality and choose the smallest permitted integer. Check that term and its predecessor.

Simple interest adds the same amount each year when the rate and original principal are fixed: $A=P(1+rt)$ for principal $P$, annual decimal rate $r$ and $t$ years. This differs from compound interest on a changing balance.
A real data set may not have exactly equal differences. Estimate a reasonable common difference, explain the modelling choice and recognise that predictions are approximate.

needs: Linear relationships and constant rate of change
leadsTo: Building a model from a pattern

misc.better: $u_{10}$ is the tenth term; $S_{10}$ is the sum of the first ten terms.

misc.weak: The sum from $k=4$ to $k=10$ contains 6 terms.
misc.better: Both endpoints count, so it contains $10-4+1=7$ terms.
Subtract only the first three terms: $S_{10}-S_3$.

misc.weak: A negative common difference means the terms form a geometric sequence.
misc.better: A constant difference can be negative. A geometric sequence has a constant ratio.

misc.weak: Simple interest at 3% of the principal each year is modelled by $A=P(1.03)^t$.
misc.better: That expression models annual compounding. Simple interest at 3% of the original principal is $A=P(1+0.03t)$.

terms.text: Write a formula in $n$ and check that it produces the given terms.
State which terms are included, choose the sum formula and identify the number of terms.
Solve the inequality, then choose and check the smallest permitted integer in context.

formula.text: Arithmetic series: $S_n=\frac n2[2u_1+(n-1)d]=\frac n2(u_1+u_n)$. Use consistent first-term and term-number conventions.

worked.prompt: A school hall has 120 seats in its first row. Each successive row has 15 more seats than the preceding row. There are 10 rows.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Find the number of seats in the tenth row.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Find the total number of seats in the hall.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Find the total number of seats in rows 4 through 10.
parts.a: $u_4=165$. There are $10-4+1=7$ rows, so the total is $\frac72(165+255)=1470$ seats.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Find the first row with more than 250 seats.
parts.a: $120+15(n-1)>250$ gives $n>9.666\ldots$. The first permitted integer is $n=10$; row 9 has 240 seats and row 10 has 255.

parts.label: (e)
parts.q: In a separate experiment, four consecutive measurements are 2.0, 5.1, 8.0 and 11.2. Use the average change between the first and fourth measurements to predict the fifth.
parts.a: There are three intervals, so the average change is $(11.2-2.0)/3=3.0666\ldots$. Adding this to the fourth value gives approximately 14.3. Because the observed differences are not equal, this is a model-based estimate.

kq.q: Why does the nth-term formula use $n-1$, not $n$?
kq.model: The first term is already present before any differences are added. Moving from term 1 to term $n$ requires $n-1$ steps.
$S_{10}$ includes rows 1 to 10. Subtracting $S_3$ removes only rows 1, 2 and 3.
Pair the first term with the last, the second with the next-to-last and so on. Each pair has the same total, so the average term is $(u_1+u_n)/2$.

kq.q: Does a constant difference of zero count as arithmetic?
kq.model: Yes. Each consecutive pair differs by the same value, $d=0$, even though the sequence does not increase or decrease.
